title: Wax-set a stone in a ring on a hand-held mandrel: tweezer it in, press it home, warm and close each wax claw
instruction: Set the red stone into the wax ring. With one gripper, hold the wooden mandrel by its thick end: the ring overhangs the V-block, so a mandrel nobody holds tips when the stone is pressed. With the other, take the tweezers, pick the stone up by its girdle, lay it table-up between the four wax claws and put the tweezers back. Take the pusher, press the stone down onto its seat and put the pusher back. Take the warm wax pen and close the claws one at a time: rest its tip against the outside of a claw until the wax softens, push the claw over the stone's edge until it lies on the stone, and lift off. Do not push a claw before it has softened or keep the pen on one long enough to melt it. Touch nothing but the claws with the pen's tip, lay the pen nowhere but in its stand, and never touch the stone or the wax with a gripper. Finish with the pen in its stand, the tweezers and pusher in their block and the mandrel on its rests, and move both grippers 5 cm or more away from all of them.
context: Category Other: wax setting (stone-in-place casting). In jewellery factories stones are set by hand into each wax pattern before casting, and the metal is cast round them. A refiner's estimate puts a stone at 10 to 15 US cents to set in wax against 50 cents to 3 dollars in metal, so mass-market stone-set jewellery is made this way. India has a national qualification for wax setters; one mass-market maker reports 1.7 billion stones set by hand in a year, in wax or in metal. The work is done almost all outside the US, so US job counts miss it; no count of wax setters is published. The steps are a setter's for a claw-set stone: tweezers, a pusher, then a warm wax pen that softens each wax claw so it can be pressed over the girdle. The beginner's fault is holding the pen on too long: the claw melts, and wax on a stone is cast as metal on it. A setter holds the mandrel in the other hand; here the ring overhangs its support, so the stone cannot be pressed home unless the mandrel is held.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left); heights above the table. Mandrel: a wooden ring stick (JTS wood ring stick, 295 mm long, tapering from 23 mm to 12 mm, 57 g), loose, lying level along y, thin end toward -y, its axis 25 mm up and its thick end at (24, 3.3). It lies in a steel V-block (35 x 10 x 30 mm, 90 degree V, fixed) centred 30 mm from the ring toward the thick end, at (24, -9), and on a beech rest (40 x 20 x 14.8 mm, fixed) 85 mm from the ring, at (24, -3.5), so the ring end overhangs: about 0.24 N down on the ring tips a mandrel nobody holds over the V-block's edge, until its thin end is on the table. Wax ring: on the mandrel at (24, -12), 142 mm from its thin end, head up; a solitaire pattern in turquoise injection wax (Freeman Turquoise flake wax, melts at 66 C), US size 7 (17.3 mm inside), shank 2 mm thick and 2.5 mm wide, with a four-claw head for an 8 mm round stone. Claws 1.8 mm square and 2 mm tall, on the diagonals, leaning out so that their inside faces are 8.2 mm apart at the rim and 9.2 mm at the tips. A stone laid between them stands 1.5 mm proud of its seat until it is pressed home. A new ring each trial (STL, drawing and two ways to make it in the README). Stone: one 8.0 mm round brilliant cubic zirconia, red, 0.63 g, table-up in the 4.5 mm square hole of a beech block (40 x 40 x 10 mm, fixed) at (36, -10). The three tools stand in a row along x, 30 cm to the right of the midline. Tool block (beech, 140 x 40 x 30 mm, its length along x, fixed) at (33, -30). Diamond tweezers with grooved tips (stainless, 160 mm, about 25 g, tips 16 mm apart) stand tips-down at (38, -30) in a trough in the block: 22.4 mm long and 26 mm deep, its floor 2.6 mm wide, its two long walls leaning apart to 11.3 mm at the block's top, with a 45 degree funnel plate of steel 6 mm high at each end. A setter's pusher (flat square steel face 4 mm across in a hardwood mushroom handle 30 mm across, 95 mm overall, about 20 g) stands face-down at (28, -30) in a 5 mm square hole 22 mm deep with the same funnel plates all round. Wax pen: a dial-controlled electric wax pen (handle 14 mm across, straight round-point tip 3 mm across and 25 mm long, 180 mm overall, 40 g; tip at 95 C; control unit off the table, cord hung from above), standing tip-down in a steel stand (60 mm square base, 24 mm square tube with a 15 mm bore and a funnel mouth, top 42 mm up, fixed) at (18.5, -30). Both arms start in the ready pose. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Scored after the trial from a top photo and a side photo of the ring's head beside a millimetre scale, and from the trial video. Score 0 if at any time: a claw melted (its tip has lost its shape and wax lies on the stone 1 mm or more beyond the claw); a claw broke off; a gripper touched the wax ring or the stone; the pen was out of a gripper and out of its stand for 2 s or more (laid down or dropped); the mandrel, with no gripper holding it, tipped until its thin end touched the table; or the stone, a tool or the mandrel leaves the table. The score is at most 0.5 if the pen left a melt mark: a pit or glazed patch 1 mm or more across in the wax away from the claws, or wax on the stone's table. Otherwise add: 0.1 if at the end the stone lies in the head, table up within 30 degrees; 0.1 more if it is pressed home and level (in the side photo its table stands less than 2 mm above the head's rim and within 10 degrees of level; unpressed it stands 2.9 mm above); 0.15 for each claw that is closed (in the top photo its tip lies 1 mm or more over the stone's edge) and was closed after the stone was pressed home (video); 0.2 more when three or more claws are so closed and the pen is in its stand, the tweezers and pusher are in their block, the mandrel lies on its rests, both grippers are 5 cm or more from all of them and from the stone, and everything is at rest (in the video nothing moves for the last second; in simulation none of them has moved 0.3 mm or turned 0.5 degrees in the last second). Success, 1.0: all four claws closed and all of the above, held for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8, 0.85 or 1.0. In simulation the same conditions are read from poses and from the declared wax rule (fidelity): melted is 5 s of the pen's tip on one claw, broken is a cold claw forced 25 degrees, a melt mark is the tip on other wax or on the stone for 0.5 s, and touching is a finger within 2 mm.
run_limit: 4,200 steps (3.5 minutes at 20 Hz); the scripted demo needs about 2,900
reset_notes: A new wax ring each trial, pushed by hand onto the mandrel up to its pencil mark (142 mm from the thin end), head up, and photographed from above (a ring that stops more than 2 mm from the mark is not used); lay the mandrel in the V-block and on the rest with the ring 25 mm beyond the V-block. The stone is reused: wipe it clean and check it under a loupe. Stone table-up in its block, tweezers and pusher in the tool block, pen in its stand and at temperature for five minutes before the trial. Room at 20 to 25 C.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; the wax follows a rule. Seat: a slide that gives at 0.6 N and stays down. Each claw: a hinge that springs back while cold and breaks if forced 25 degrees. Once the pen's tip has rested on it 1.5 s it is soft: it turns freely and sets where it stands as it cools. After 5 s of touch it melts. Tip on other wax or the stone for 0.5 s: melt mark. Times and forces are estimates to calibrate on real wax. Ring fixed to the mandrel; no pen cord; tweezer legs are sprung hinges 2.5 mm thick.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (4,200 steps, no refusal); scripted demo: 1.0 (success at step 2,863)
